This can be accomplished by either adding a 57,000 kW unit to an existing power plant or by adding 57,000 kW to the planned size of a future unit.
6.07 Natural Gas. Natural gas is the most environmentally acceptable fuel since the stack emissins are very low in pollutants, and there is no ash. It is the fuel most widely used now to serve the south Texas market, but it is becoming prohibitively expensive for power generation and frequently is not available at all. There is a moratorium on constructing new gas-fired power plants to allow diverting what remains of this clean burning fuel to higher and (or) better uses. Because of its short supply, high cost, and the moratorium, it is not a viable alternative to the proposed action. Amistad hydropower could conserve about 3.1 billion cubic feet of natural gas per year, exclusive of the pumping energy necessary to move the gas from the field to the power plant.
6.08 Fuel Oil. Fuel oil is also a relatively clean burning fuel that leaves virtually no residue. Fuel oils refined from domestic crudes are in almost as short supply as natural gas. Imported crudes are becoming increasingly expensive. As demand increases for electrical energy, major oil companies report that additional refining capacity is not available. Fuel oil is not a viable alternative for the same reasons as for natural gas for the additional reason that it will require importation of foreign oil, which is not in accordance with the national self-sufficiency goal. Amistad hydropower would conserve (or preclude importation of) about 625,000 barrels of crude oil per year exclusive of the oil that would be used to transport it to the power plant.
6.09 Coal. High quality coal deposits (as opposed to lignite, which is low quality) occur in Webb County as noted in paragraph 2.12, but they are not extensive enough to construct a "mine mouth" power plant. It may be that these deposits of cannel coal are more valuable for other uses than as furnace fuel. As previously noted, CP&L plans to construct new units totaling 1,100 MW capacity, using Wyoming (or Montana) coal, scheduled for service in 1979 and 1986. This type plant is usually considered base-load. Whereas a base-load plant will not perform efficiently when used as a peaking unit, hydropower is the most efficient peaking power. According to a Federal Power Commission study of 1974, "The combustion of coal results in emission to the atmosphere of oxides of sulfur and nitrogen, as well as fly ash. The fly ash emission can be controlled by known methods. However, processes for removal of sulfur oxides are in only a commercial testing stage, and many difficulties have appeared." Of 24 stack gas installations at coal-fired power plants of 150 MW or larger in the United States, none was in satisfactory operation in 1974. In the short term, power produced from burning coal is not as acceptable as is Amistad hydropower. The proposed improvement will prevent the necessity to use about 482,000 tons of coal per year, exclusive of the energy necessary to transport it from northern states to south Texas.
6.10 Lignite. There are deposits of lignite in south Texas as noted in paragraph 2.12. The lignite-fired power plant to be constructed by the Medina-South Texas-Brazos Electric Co-ops will be located at Tilden, McMullen County, Texas. The lignite deposit is immediately adjacent. Two examples of this type plant would be the plants at Fairfield and at Mount Vernon, Texas. In the case of the power plant at Fairfield (named Big Brown), the lignite is open-pit mined about 2 or 3 miles from the plant and is transported to the furnace by large trucks. In the case of the power plant near Mount Vernon (named Monticello), the lignite is open-pit mined and moved about 7 miles to the powerhouse by rail.
